item.title: Analytically Benchmarked Spatial and Temporal Discretization Guidelines for Finite Element Simulation of Thermal Waves
item.description: arXiv:2610.20938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite element simulation is widely used to design and interpret thermal wave-based measurement systems. The accuracy of the results obtained from such simulations depends on how finely the model is resolved in space and time. The discretization resolution is often chosen case by case rather than following a well-defined guideline. This work recommends a discretization protocol for finite element simulation of thermal waves where the spatial discretization is scaled to the thermal diffusion length and the temporal discretization to the number of time steps per cycle. The associated discretization errors are quantified using three benchmark problems of increasing complexity. The spatial phase error converges at second order in the element size, reaching 0.14 degrees at ten elements per diffusion length, whereas the temporal error decreases only at first order in the number of time steps per cycle; thus, the time step can be set from a target phase tolerance $\epsilon$. Each error is assessed against a reference that isolates it. The benchmark case with subsurface defects shows the consequence of violating the recommended discretization protocol.
item.dc:creator: Kaushal Arun Pareek, Daniel May, Peter Meszmer, Bernhard Wunderle, Mohamad Abo Ras

item.title: Acoustic Illusion of a Rigid Object for a Moving Emitter via Equivalent Surface Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.21649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report a three-dimensional acoustic illusion of a rigid object illuminated by an emitter moving along an arbitrary trajectory. The object is absent: control sources are arranged around its location, the closed surface they define being termed the equivalent surface. Driven by the field the object would have scattered onto this surface, the sources radiate, by the Kirchhoff--Helmholtz representation, that same field beyond it. The control signals follow in closed form from a time-dependent physical optics formulation that we derive for a moving emitter, in which the motion enters analytically through the acoustic travel times, so that the scattering problem need not be re-solved at each emitter position, nor the propagation domain discretized. For objects too large to enclose, the signals are mapped onto an internal surface, an option whose advantages and penalties are discussed. Numerical simulations validate the method in both configurations.
item.dc:creator: Asaf Kor, Lea Beilkin-Sirota

item.title: Plasma-Enabled Wideband Matching of Electrically Small Antennas
item.description: arXiv:2610.22095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a plasma-based approach for wideband impedance matching of electrically small antennas (ESAs). By exploiting the negative permittivity of a capacitively coupled plasma (CCP), the plasma is shown to function as a wideband negative capacitor that effectively compensates for the large and frequency-dependent reactance inherent to ESAs. A VHF/UHF electrically small capped dipole antenna is used as a proof-of-concept platform to demonstrate the proposed technique. Theoretical analysis, Multiphysics simulations, and experimental measurements confirm broadband impedance matching, with -6 dB fractional bandwidth that can exceed 100\%, using only a few watts of plasma power. The matching bandwidth can be dynamically tuned by adjusting the plasma operating conditions, gas pressure, and electron density, enabling control over the trade-off between bandwidth and radiation efficiency. This plasma-enabled matching paradigm provides a physically robust and scalable solution for wideband ESAs, particularly attractive for low-frequency and high-power applications where conventional matching techniques are fundamentally limited.
item.dc:creator: Kushagra Singhal, Abbas Semnani

item.title: The role of friction on heave-induced motion of offshore drilling systems: modelling, analysis, and numerical experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.22189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the influence of friction dynamics on heave-induced disturbance propagation using a coupled hydraulic-structural drilling model formulated as a semilinear interconnection of ordinary and hyperbolic partial differential equations (ODE-PDEs), and capturing spatially distributed memory effects in the drillstring-wellbore interaction. First, local and global existence and uniqueness results are established, and sufficient conditions for boundedness and input-to-state stability are deduced via a small-gain analysis. Subsequently, extensive numerical investigations are carried out, including harmonic excitation studies, nonlinear distortion analysis, spatial amplification investigations, mechanism-isolation experiments, parameter sensitivity analysis, and broadband simulations under realistic offshore sea-state excitation. The simulation results indicate that, whilst the hydraulic response is governed primarily by wave propagation phenomena, compressibility, and boundary reflections, the structural dynamics display substantially greater sensitivity to distributed friction effects. Furthermore, drillstring-wellbore friction is shown to have a relatively limited influence on well-posedness but a potentially significant impact on stability margins. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for coupled hydraulic-structural dynamics and distributed friction mechanisms when analysing, monitoring, and controlling offshore drilling systems.
item.dc:creator: Luigi Romano, Ole Morten Aamo

item.title: Weber-number scaling and the distance dependence of drop size in full-cone pressure-swirl sprays
item.description: arXiv:2610.20650v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A pressure-swirl nozzle converts the feed pressure into a swirling conical sheet that breaks into ligaments and then into drops. The size of the drops governs the deposition and drift of agricultural sprays, the capture of airborne dust and the combustion efficiency of fuel injectors. The standard tool for measuring the drop size is laser diffraction, which returns a spatial, concentration-weighted distribution at the beam station. However, the dependence of the measured drop size on the nozzle-to-beam distance has not been quantified alongside a Weber-number scaling, so prefactors reported at different distances cannot be compared on an equal footing. To this end, we measure the drop-size distribution of two full-cone pressure-swirl nozzles by laser diffraction at a range of distances, pressures and orientations, together with high-speed imaging of the sheet breakup. We find that the volume-median diameter $D_{v50}$ decreases with the measurement distance $L$ as $D_{v50} \sim L^{-0.18}$ beyond the drop-formation region. A joint fit over both nozzles gives $D_{v50}/d_0 \sim \mathrm{We}^{-0.31}\,(L/d_0)^{-0.21}$, where $d_0$ is the orifice diameter and $\mathrm{We}$ the Weber number, which separates the pressure and distance effects. At a fixed distance the two nozzles collapse onto the $\mathrm{We}^{-1/3}$ scaling of Kooij et al. (2018), and the measured distance dependence may account for part of the offset between our near-field prefactor and the far-field value. Thus, a drop size obtained by laser diffraction is meaningful only when the measurement distance is reported with it, and a spray should be characterized at the actual distance between the nozzle and its target.
item.dc:creator: Bilal Ben Jemaa, Vincent He, Marko Trifunovi\'c, Daniel Duke, Rishabh V. More

item.title: Global-in-time Spectral Duhamel-Picard Method for Post-Exposure Bake Simulation and Physics-Informed Neural Operators for EUV Lithography
item.description: arXiv:2610.20655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a global-in-time spectral Duhamel-Picard method with polynomial expansions for post-exposure bake (PEB) simulation. The coupled acid-quencher reaction-diffusion equations are reformulated as nonlinear Volterra integral equations using the Duhamel principle. Full trajectories are represented by finite polynomial expansions, with temporal coefficient fields determined over the bake interval by Anderson-accelerated Picard iteration, thereby avoiding sequential time marching. In 3-D PEB simulations, we employ Chebyshev and Legendre temporal bases while evaluating the Duhamel integrals using the corresponding Gaussian quadrature rules. We demonstrate that the proposed method simulates a large domain of $1200\times1200\times100$ voxels on the order of one minute. The representation is further incorporated into a physics-informed neural operator (PINO) with a mixed-transform variant of a factorized Fourier neural operator, which is trained without precomputed solution trajectories. Together, the integral formulation and its PINO extension enable accelerated, time-marching-free prediction of concentration fields at arbitrary times within the bake interval.
item.dc:creator: Doyun Kim, Mircea Dusa, Werner Gilijns, Philippe Leray

item.title: Thermal Confinement in Plasmonic Nanoparticles under Generalised Pulsed Illumination
item.description: arXiv:2610.21698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Thermal confinement is a key parameter in photothermal applications, as it determines the spatial extent of the region affected by the generated heat. In this work, we develop a numerical treatment to quantify thermal confinement in spherical plasmonic nanoparticles under excitation conditions ranging from ultrashort pulses to the continuous-wave regime. The model combines generalized optical heating with a finite-difference solution of the transient heat equation and explicitly accounts for finite interfacial thermal conductance. To characterize the spatial distribution of heat, we introduce a thermal confinement radius defined from the temporal temperature envelope in the surrounding medium. We demonstrate that pulse duration acts as a highly effective, tuneable parameter to govern thermal confinement. Notably, we quantitatively show that finite interfacial thermal conductance can induce deviations of up to 20% in the spatial confinement radius and over 60% in the transient thermal construct under ultrashort excitation. By comparing the characteristic dimensions of representative targeting ligands with the resulting thermal-confinement length scales, we show how pulse duration can be precisely tailored to control target heating. These results provide a unified framework for predicting nanoscale heat localization paving the way for the rational design of high precision thermoplasmonic applications.
item.dc:creator: Javier Gonz\'alez-Colsa, Dolores Ortiz, Jos\'e Mar\'ia Saiz, Alfredo Franco, Francisco Gonz\'alez, Fernando Bresme, Pablo Albella

item.title: Large in-plane optical anisotropy in epitaxial CrN(113) films
item.description: arXiv:2610.21856v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: CrN, a transition-metal nitride crystallizing in the cubic rocksalt structure, exhibits a unique combination of mechanical robustness, semiconducting behavior, and thermoelectric functionality. To date, however, CrN has been synthesized primarily as polycrystalline material or as epitaxial films grown along high-symmetry orientations such as (001) and (111). Here, we prepare epitaxial CrN(113) films on AlN(11\bar{2}2) templates by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy. The low-symmetry interface and highly direction dependent lattice mismatch are expected to modify the physical properties of CrN relative to the bulk material. Indeed, variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry in the photon-energy range from 1.25 to 5 eV reveals a surprisingly strong polarization dependence of the optical response despite the nearly strain-free cubic crystal structure of the films. The pseudo-optical constants n and k differ by more than 10% for orthogonal in-plane polarizations throughout the investigated spectral range. We evaluate possible origins of this effect and conclude that it most likely arises from anisotropic surface morphology of CrN(113), which creates a metasurface acting as a subwavelength grating in the strongly absorbing regime.
item.dc:creator: Duc V. Dinh, Frank Peiris, Oliver Brandt

item.title: De-Risking Robotic Welding for In-Space Metal Joining Through Physics-Grounded Digital Twins
item.description: arXiv:2610.21939v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Growing interest in in-space servicing, manufacturing, and assembly has renewed attention on reliable metal joining for modular construction and on-orbit repair. Robotic welding is promising, but reduced-gravity and low-pressure operation remains poorly characterised and flight-like tests are limited. The UK Space Agency-supported ISPARK project is developing a physics-grounded digital twin for structured process de-risking. This paper evaluates a model-based prototype combining a finite-volume thermal weld-pool model, Gaussian-process (GP) and neural-network surrogates, and a simulated six-axis manipulator. The reduced model includes solid-liquid phase change, effective thermocapillary transport, and a local-pressure parameter. Gravity is assessed separately through a hydrostatic-to-capillary pressure ratio and does not enter the thermal energy equation. Across repeated five-fold cross-validation, the GP has lower normalised mean absolute error than the neural network for all eight outputs. In 10 held-out boundary cases, 74 of 80 solver responses fall within nominal 90% GP predictive intervals. A three-output GP query takes 249 microseconds, including scaling and predictive variance. In a simulated UR5 L-shaped-seam study, a proportional controller adjusts the synergic power-source setting as travel speed falls near the corner. Finite-volume re-evaluation finds all 12 closed-loop operating points and 9 of 12 open-loop points within an illustrative 1.0-3.0 mm root-side-width band. These simulation results support using the framework to screen welding conditions and control strategies before experimental tests. Thermal-vacuum, targeted reduced-gravity, and robotic hardware-in-the-loop studies are needed to assess the model and controller.
item.dc:creator: Zhou Daniel Hao, Umer Masood Chaudry, Robert Shaw, Andrew Cheney, Nick Ludford, Mark Sims, Hongbiao Dong

item.title: Empirical Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization from Encoded Unitary Designs
item.description: arXiv:2511.14296v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce the Constraint-Enhanced Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (CE-QAOA), a shallow, constraint-aware ansatz that operates inside the one-hot product space [n]^m, where m is the number of blocks and each block is initialized in an n-qubit W_n state. We give an ancilla-free, depth-optimal encoder that prepares W_n using n-1 two-qubit rotations per block, and a two-local block-XY mixer that preserves the one-hot manifold and has a constant spectral gap on the one-excitation sector. At the level of expressivity, we establish per-block controllability, implying approximate universality per block. At the level of distributional behavior, we show that, after natural block and symbol permutation twirls, shallow CE-QAOA realizes an encoded unitary 1-design and supports approximate second-moment (2-design) behavior; combined with a Paley-Zygmund argument, this yields finite-shot anticoncentration guarantees. Algorithmically, we wrap constant-depth sampling with a deterministic feasibility checker to obtain a polynomial-time hybrid quantum-classical solver (PHQC) that returns the best observed feasible solution in O(S n^2) time, where S is a polynomial shot budget. We obtain two advantages. First, when CE-QAOA fixes r >= 1 locations different from the start city, we achieve a Theta(n^r) reduction in shot complexity even against a classical sampler that draws uniformly from the feasible set. Second, against a classical baseline restricted to raw bitstring sampling, we show an exp(Theta(n^2)) minimax separation. In noiseless circuit simulations of traveling salesman problem instances with n in {4,...,10} locations from the QOPTLib benchmark library, we recover the global optimum at depth p = 1 using polynomial shot budgets and coarse parameter grids defined by the problem size.
item.dc:creator: Chinonso Onah, Roman Firt, Kristel Michielsen

item.title: Absorption and Phase-Contrast Microtomography Using Direct X-Ray Detection With Commercial Off-The-Shelf CMOS Sensors
item.description: arXiv:2605.29808v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work presents high-resolution X-ray microtomography based on commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) CMOS image sensors as direct detectors. The system uses a microfocus X-ray source in cone-beam geometry, enabling both absorption-contrast imaging, thanks to the sensor s intrinsic resolution, and phase-contrast imaging, by adjusting the object-to-sensor distance. A dynamic flat-field correction algorithm mitigates radiation-induced sensor degradation during long acquisitions. The setup provides voxel sizes from 3.9 microns to 5.2 microns, with an effective spatial resolution (FWHM) as fine as 9.6 microns in magnified phase-contrast mode (1.33x) and 21 microns in non-magnified absorption-contrast mode. Phase contrast enhances visualization of soft tissue boundaries that are difficult to visualize using absorption-contrast imaging in the same experimental configuration.
item.dc:creator: Damian L. Corzi, Jose Lipovetzky, Fabricio Alcalde Bessia, German Mato, Andres Cicuttin, Maria L. Crespo, Martin Perez, Mariano Gomez Berisso

item.title: Picometre-scale real-time drift correction in TEM and STEM by dynamic control of the specimen stage for atomic-resolution imaging
item.description: arXiv:2608.03344v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we show how the specimen drift can be actively compensated by controlling the stage with precision down to the picometre scale. We do this by dynamic control, a generic real-time feedback framework designed to actively stabilize electron microscopy experiments by continuously monitoring an experimental variable from the detector data stream and compensating its evolution during acquisition. The framework, applicable to a broad range of controllable experimental instabilities, includes automated calibration procedures, operates in parallel with image acquisition and is implemented as a software plugin without requiring any hardware modification of the microscope. Results for live drift correction are shown for a selection of TEM and STEM instruments using conventional mechanical stages as well as piezoelectric stages. Experimental results are presented for medium resolution TEM, high-resolution TEM, HR-STEM and in situ observations. With piezoelectric stages, specimen stabilization down to the picometre scale was achieved allowing drift-corrected atomic-resolution imaging. Specimen stage-based stabilization significantly improves long-exposure imaging and in situ experiments by increasing the effective exposure time, preserving the field of view, maintaining identical optical conditions and eliminating the need for numerical alignment of large datasets. Beyond the specific application presented here, dynamic control provides a versatile framework for real-time regulation of electron microscopy experiments and opens new perspectives for quantitative imaging, automated in situ studies and multimodal acquisitions.
item.dc:creator: Christophe Gatel, Julien Dupuy, Teresa Hungria, Martin J. Hytch

item.title: Braided endovascular implants for intracranial aneurysms: mechanics, hemodynamics, and clinical translation
item.description: arXiv:2609.18544v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Endovascular implants prevent intracranial aneurysm rupture by altering the mechanical and hemodynamic environment at the aneurysm neck. Yet many in silico workflows prescribe or reconstruct the post-deployment geometry before computing flow, leaving unresolved the mechanics that create the clinically relevant interface. Here we review braided intraluminal flow diverters, intrasaccular devices, and emerging flow-disruption concepts across deployment mechanics, inter-wire and wire-wall contact, superelasticity, wall apposition, pore geometry, computational fluid dynamics, and fluid-structure interaction. We connect these modeling choices to neck coverage, malapposition, migration, deformation, and durability, and distinguish established evidence from mechanistic inference and prospective hypotheses. We argue that model fidelity should match the clinical question: prescribed or fast placement may support screening, whereas questions of coverage, apposition, compaction, and migration benefit from mechanically plausible deployment states. An interface-resolved mechanics-to-flow framework, supported by measurable validation targets and standardized reporting, could improve device design and enable more reliable patient-specific treatment planning.
item.dc:creator: Ratnadeep Pramanik, Duygu Dengiz, Mariya S. Pravdivtseva, Martin Frank, Ivo Steinbrecher, Prasanth Velvaluri, Matthias Mayr, Philipp Berg, Sylvia Saalfeld, Naomi Larsen, Olav Jansen, Alexander Popp
